incidents.title: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.title_en: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.summary:
Angela Lipps, 50, of Tennessee, was arrested at gunpoint in July 2025 and spent about six months in jail after being falsely charged with bank theft in Fargo, North Dakota. US marshals took her from her home while she babysat a neighbor's four children. She was held nearly four months in Tennessee awaiting extradition, then about two more months in North Dakota. Charges were dropped after her lawyer provided bank records proving she was in Tennessee at the time. She was released on Christmas Eve and later learned she had lost her residence, car, and personal property.

Lipps is now suing the city of Fargo and police detective Lucas Heck for $10m in federal court. The lawsuit says police relied on an AI facial recognition match from a fake ID and her social media photo, then sought an arrest warrant without enough investigation or probable cause. It also claims the department lacked proper policies, training, and supervision for facial recognition technology. Fargo officials declined to comment on pending litigation. The suit seeks accountability and more careful use of such technology.

incidents.title: Former Costa Mesa Police Officer Pleads Guilty to Contacting His Mistress Thousands of Times Through Text, Phone Calls, and Social Media Messages, Including More than 100 Times in a Day, Illegally Accessing Confidential Law Enforcement Databases to Track Romantic Rivals, Ex-girlfriend, and Wife
incidents.title_en: Former Costa Mesa Police Officer Pleads Guilty to Contacting His Mistress Thousands of Times Through Text, Phone Calls, and Social Media Messages, Including More than 100 Times in a Day, Illegally Accessing Confidential Law Enforcement Databases to Track Romantic Rivals, Ex-girlfriend, and Wife
incidents.summary:
Former Costa Mesa police officer Robert Jay Josett, 35, pleaded guilty to three misdemeanors, including unauthorized computer access, repeated annoying phone calls, and violating a restraining order. After his mistress ended their relationship, he contacted her thousands of times by text, phone, and social media over nine months, sometimes more than 100 times in one day. He also called her and her new boyfriend up to 58 times in a single day and repeatedly drove past her home.

Josett used the California Law Enforcement Telecommunications System to make 13 unauthorized inquiries about his mistress, a romantic rival, and his wife, and he accessed the police department's license plate reader system to track vehicles. After being served with a protective order and notice of termination on June 28, 2024, he drove by her house and was arrested. He was sentenced to three years informal probation and a 52-week domestic violence program, and his law enforcement certification review is pending.

incidents.title: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.title_en: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.summary:
Two sisters from Rio Arriba County are suing Española after a July 23 traffic stop. Jaclynn Gonzales, 21, was driving with her 12-year-old sister when a Flock Safety camera misread their license plate, confusing a final 2 for a 7 and flagging the car as stolen from Rio Rancho. Officers stopped them on Calle Duran, handcuffed both, and placed them in separate police cars before realizing the error. Jaclynn asked police to call their mother, who lived nearby, to pick up the girl, but officers instead handcuffed the child and put her in another vehicle.

The lawsuits, filed Jan. 3 in state District Court, seek unspecified damages for anxiety, fear, and restriction of movement. Their attorney, Sheri Raphaelson, also represents Adam Pacheco, who was 17 when he was wrongly stopped in a similar camera-related mistake in April. The city, police chief, and Flock Safety did not respond to requests for comment. No next steps are stated beyond the pending lawsuits.

incidents.title: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.title_en: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.summary:
Rebecca Green agreed to let an AI scribe transcribe her first urologist appointment, but the tool invented a claim that she used psychedelic mushrooms. She found the false statement in a letter sent to her GP after kidney stone surgery in March. Because she was receiving workers' compensation, she feared the error could hurt her case. After she complained, the urologist apologized, corrected the record, and said she would review how AI was used in her practice.

The article says about 40 percent of Australian GPs regularly use AI scribes, though none are approved by the medical device regulator. A privacy watchdog report found other serious mistakes, such as recording the wrong breast in a cancer diagnosis. The Therapeutic Goods Administration has been reviewing these tools and will release findings in the coming weeks, with breaches to be acted on. Patient advocates want approved lists and stronger checks, while Ms Green says she would only consent again with a doctor she already knows.

incidents.title: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.title_en: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.summary:
A 37-year-old Vero Beach man named Peter Solomon Ruma was arrested after police say he used artificial intelligence to create and share explicit images of women without their permission. He reportedly took photos from social media and other online sources to make the altered images. Investigators searched his home and electronic devices on Wednesday and found evidence linking him to the activity. Ruma is being held on a $1 million bond and faces eight charges connected to one female victim between June and August 2026, including three counts of creating altered sexual depictions, three counts of promoting them, one count of sexual cyber harassment, and one count of stalking.

Police have identified several additional possible victims who may not know images of them were made or shared, and they believe Ruma may have done this for years. The investigation is ongoing and more charges could be filed. Authorities are asking anyone who thinks they were victimized or has information about the images to contact the Vero Beach Police Department.

incidents.title: L'homme qui a attaqué une garderie suisse a trouvé ses victimes sur ChatGPT
incidents.title_en: The man who attacked a Swiss daycare found his victims on ChatGPT
incidents.summary:
A 23-year-old Chinese student is on trial in Zurich for attempted murder after stabbing three five-year-old boys on 1 October 2024 in Oerlikon. He used a knife with an 8.5 centimetre blade, seriously injuring all three. One boy had a vein at his collarbone completely cut and needed emergency surgery, another was stabbed twice in the chest and nearly died from heart and blood vessel damage, and the third suffered wounds to his ear and lung. A childcare worker grabbed the attacker's arms, making him drop the knife and surrender until police arrived.

Prosecutors say he planned the attack for weeks, using ChatGPT to ask about legal consequences of stabbing random victims and choosing children as targets. He bought clothes and a set of kitchen knives, studied anatomy, and bought raw beef to practise stabbing the day before. The prosecution describes him as extremely cold-blooded and motivated by revenge, a need for attention, and ideological delusion. He is due in court on Thursday, where prosecutors are demanding a 15-year prison sentence and a 15-year expulsion from Switzerland.

incidents.title: Masked AI call forces Parkview High into soft lockdown
incidents.title_en: Masked AI call forces Parkview High into soft lockdown
incidents.summary:
Parkview High School in Gwinnett County, Georgia received its fourth AI-generated bomb threat of the school year on Monday. School officials placed the school on lockdown out of an abundance of caution, and it later returned to normal operations. The latest threat involved a masked phone number, which follows a pattern seen in recent threats, according to a letter sent to parents by school police.

Gwinnett County Public Schools police are now working with the Georgia Bureau of Investigation and the FBI to determine who is responsible for the threats. Investigators are looking for the source of the threats. No arrests have been announced and no suspect has been identified. The investigation is ongoing, but authorities have not said what will happen next.

stories.Headline: Vyzoxa Redefines AI Learning Through Practical AI Agent Development, Empowering Learners Worldwide to Build With Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Vyzoxa, an education technology platform run by NDFM Business World Pvt. Ltd., has introduced a practical artificial intelligence learning pathway. It aims to help one million people become AI innovators by 2030. Participants first complete about two weeks of AI agent industrial training with recorded lessons and daily tasks. They then move into a four week project based internship in AI agent development at no extra cost, where they build and present a working AI agent. The program is remote and self paced, open to learners in India and many international regions.

The platform includes AI tools called Vyzoxa Intelligent Systems, such as an AI mentor, AI coder, and AI engine, to support learning and project work. Founder Mansajan Singh and Managing Director Gurjinder Singh lead the company. For eligible participants in India, top performers may be shortlisted for a final interview and could receive employment or pre-placement offers, but these are performance based and not guaranteed. The article does not state a specific next step beyond the platform's ongoing mission and enrollment.

stories.Headline: B.C. government sues OpenAI over Tumbler Ridge mass shooting - The Globe and Mail
stories.Summary:
British Columbia has sued OpenAI in a California federal court over the February mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge. The province says 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar killed eight victims, including five students aged 12 and 13, an educational assistant, and her mother and brother, before taking her own life. Attorney General Niki Sharma said ChatGPT had alarming conversations with the shooter that triggered an internal review, but OpenAI never warned the RCMP and has refused to share the chats.

The lawsuit names CEO Sam Altman and related entities as defendants, accusing them of negligence, aiding a mass shooting, and selling a defective product. It seeks damages above $75,000, plus punitive amounts, and reimbursement for costs such as a new school and mental health support. British Columbia and Ottawa have already committed $200 million for a new school and health centre upgrades. The province is also asking the court to order OpenAI to add safeguards that end or de-escalate violent conversations.

stories.Headline: Gov. Pritzker Establishes Illinois Artificial Intelligence (AI) Cabinet - RiverBender.com
stories.Summary:
Governor JB Pritzker signed Executive Order 2026-07 to create an Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet. This group will include experts from academia, law, ethics, governance, and state agencies such as emergency management, public health, and technology. It will assess risks AI poses to residents, advise on preparing for and responding to AI incidents, and recommend safeguards for public buildings, water systems, and information infrastructure. The order follows earlier state AI safety laws and comes amid federal inaction and a recent whistleblower resignation.

The cabinet will also evaluate possible regulatory steps, including tying data center tax incentives to safety standards, addressing energy burdens on the grid, and considering strict liability for AI caused harm. Governor Pritzker will seek input from agency leaders and announce appointed members in the coming weeks. Lieutenant Governor Juliana Stratton and University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Chancellor Charles Isbell voiced support.

stories.Headline: Trump Orders US Government to Replace 'Artificial Intelligence' With 'Super Intelligence' in Official Documents - finance.biggo.com
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump told the United Nations General Assembly that all US government documents will now say "Super Intelligence" instead of "artificial intelligence," effective immediately. He said the word "artificial" makes the technology sound fake and hoped other countries would adopt the new term. The change follows his Truth Social post asking followers to choose a replacement. This conflicts with researchers, who use "superintelligence" for a hypothetical future system that exceeds human ability, not current AI.

The move fits the administration's push to speed up AI development and limit regulation, including an executive order barring mandatory licensing and a memo urging national security agencies to adopt advanced AI faster. On Monday, 22 countries backed a declaration calling for AI to remain under human control, but the United States and China did not sign. The article does not say what specific federal documents will change next, though Trump has signaled he may challenge state AI rules in court.

stories.Headline: Trump rejects calls for int'l regulation on AI-Xinhua
stories.Summary:
At the 81st United Nations General Assembly, U.S. President Donald Trump rejected international calls to regulate artificial intelligence. He said the United States would only encourage AI development and keep its leadership role in a safe and responsible way. Trump argued that global control efforts would stifle a technology he believes will be larger than the industrial revolution. He said the Department of Justice would monitor AI closely, and he suggested renaming artificial intelligence as "super intelligence."

Earlier the same day, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that humans are handing power to machines, with AI agents going rogue and lethal autonomous weapons becoming a military reality. He urged leading AI countries to share safety information and create a multilateral risk management framework. Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva also called for regulation of Big Tech and AI, saying technology should not develop without rules, transparency, or ethical boundaries. Several U.S. AI industry leaders had recently asked for a coordinated slowdown of AI development.

stories.Headline: AI shopping bots raise scam, fraud, data-privacy risks, banks warn
stories.Summary:
Banks including NatWest, Bank of America, ING, Capital One and Commonwealth Bank of Australia warned on Tuesday that using AI agents for online shopping could increase scams, fraud and data privacy breaches. They issued principles as tech companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta promote chatbots that can select products and make purchases. British retailer John Lewis said AI agent searches rose to 2.5 percent from 0.3 percent a year earlier.

The banks said customers are keen but the technology is moving faster than consumer protections. Risks include AI agents taking card details and entering them directly into websites, or pushing users toward payment methods with weaker safeguards. The banks plan to discuss proposals with policymakers, including disclosure when an AI agent is involved, more transparency over decisions, data safeguards, and allowing consumers and merchants to choose interoperable AI shopping services.

stories.Headline: Google Fined More Than €400 Million by Irish Regulator Over Location Data Privacy Breaches
stories.Summary:
Google has been fined more than €400 million, about £345 million, by Ireland's Data Protection Commission for breaching EU privacy rules on location data. The investigation began six years ago after complaints from European consumer rights groups and covered May 2018 to February 2020. It focused on three Google features: web and app activity, location history, and location accuracy. The regulator found that users may not have understood their location information was being used for targeted advertising or to infer their interests, raising concerns about transparency.

Along with the fine, Google must bring its location data practices into compliance with GDPR within six months. This is the fourth largest penalty imposed by the Irish regulator since GDPR took effect in May 2018. The decision adds to regulatory pressure on technology companies over how they collect and use personal location data for advertising and user profiling.

stories.Headline: The Narrow Path to a Trump-Xi AI Deal
stories.Summary:
Britain and the United States have agreed a new defence partnership on artificial intelligence. The UK's Defence Rapid AI Delivery Taskforce will work with the US Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office to speed up deployment of trusted, interoperable AI and autonomous systems. Andy Burnham unveiled the deal in New York, saying it will strengthen deterrence and protect critical infrastructure such as airspace and vital sea lanes. The UK taskforce was launched with £100 million in funding.

Burnham will promote the agreement at the UN General Assembly and is due to meet President Donald Trump. The pact deepens transatlantic military tech ties but raises concerns about British reliance on American technology. Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey called for an international treaty to pause super-intelligent AI. Next, the two taskforces must show they can turn the agreement into deployable technology, and Britain is expected to push for wider international action when it hosts the G20 in Manchester next year.

stories.Headline: Pritzker establishes AI cabinet amid calls for greater regulation
stories.Summary:
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker signed an executive order on Tuesday creating an artificial intelligence cabinet made up of unpaid experts and state agency representatives. The group will develop policy proposals through 2027 and examine risks AI poses to residents and critical infrastructure such as water systems, education, and information networks. It will also study emerging AI incidents and recommend safety, accountability, and transparency measures, including possible conditions on data center incentives and reviews of energy grid strain.

The move follows a whistleblower's claim that AI could become uncontrollable by 2030, and it builds on Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act signed in July. That law targets AI models earning over $500 million annually, requires reporting on risks like weapons creation or cyberattacks, and mandates annual audits starting in 2028. Pritzker is urging Congress to hold hearings and set national standards, saying AI is as dangerous as nuclear weapons and needs international cooperation.

stories.Headline: Australia AI regulations: Anthropic, OpenAI call for Australia to relax ban on training of AI models
stories.Summary:
OpenAI and Anthropic have asked Australia to soften its planned ban on using local creative content to train artificial intelligence models. The two US companies made submissions to a parliamentary inquiry in September, arguing that a narrow copyright exemption could protect creators while attracting investment. Australia has already ruled out such an exemption, and its broader AI and data centre rules take effect next year. The companies say the sector could be worth hundreds of billions of dollars by the end of the decade.

Anthropic proposed a conditional approval system and said it would consider conditions that support Australian creators. OpenAI called for a balanced framework allowing models to learn from information that is publicly available while giving rightsholders chances to collaborate. Both companies linked their requests to major local projects, including an OpenAI data centre deal in Sydney and an Anthropic partnership in Queensland. The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence is due to report in November.
